newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Canberra revises proposed telecoms regulation.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Canberra revises proposed telecoms regulation.

text.p: Australian Communications Minister Richard Alston published the government's planned system of telecommunications regulation on Friday.

The system, on which the government has invited comment, will commence from in July, marking the end of the current duopoly on most telecommunications services enjoyed by Optus Communications Pty Ltd and the government's Telstra Corp.
The former Labor government had proposed a system last year, but the new Liberal-National administration's system, embodied in a draft bill issued by Alston, included these new features:
First, the market for services that telecoms companies must offer to industry newcomers will be defined by what they are already offering.
So if a new operation wants to buy capacity for resale, it will be able to refer to contracts that, say, Telstra is currently providing for someone else.

Second, the draft bill showed that a company will need to obtain a telecommunications carrier license if it has a certain sized network (a line more than 500 metres long or a total network longer than five km) and also serves customers outside its own business.
This means that a company that has its own large but entirely internal system will not be seen as a carrier.
But if it starts offering services to someone else, it will need a license.
An exception to that rule is that if a company's capacity is simply used as part of a telecoms carrier's operation, only the carrier will need the license.
Licensed carriers will have to pay fees for industry regulation and, most importantly, will have to share such facilities as underground ducts, poles, towers and system data.
An official who asked not to be named said this aspect of the system was aimed at reducing the industry costs and, notably, cutting the cost of entry for new players.
Third, regulations against restricting competition in the telecommunications industry will apply to anyone, not just to licensed carriers.
Fourth, carriers will have to let each other connect to their networks.
This, again, reduces barriers to entry, because a new operator can be assured not only of buying capacity from an existing carrier but will also be able to connect with it.
So, for example, a new players' telephone customer will be able to dial customers of an existing carrier.
